texts.https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/20/ex-opena: Ex-OpenAI executive builds $1.5 billion AI manufacturing startup Arda Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Former OpenAI employee Bob McGrew has been quietly building a startup called Arda, which raised capital at a $1.5 billion valuation. McGrew, who spent parts of his career at Palantir and PayPal, said Arda is building an AI assistant for manufacturing and has already been working with Anduril. "It's a user interface and an agent that does for manufacturing engineers what Claude or Cursor does for programmers," McGrew told CNBC. watch now VIDEO 32:15 32:15 Former top OpenAI employees raises capital for defense startup valued at $1.5B Tech OpenAI's former research chief has been quietly building a startup that aims to bring manufacturing back to the U.S. using AI. Bob McGrew's newest company, Arda, has raised $230 million at a $1.5 billion valuation, the company told CNBC in an exclusive interview Tuesday. The round was led by Altimeter Capital, Accel and Khosla Ventures. Arda makes AI software to help automate manufacturing. McGrew, who was also Palantir's product and engineering lead for over a decade, said Arda's AI models have already been deployed with military tech company Anduril. "It's a user interface and an agent that does for manufacturing engineers what Claude or Cursor does for programmers," McGrew told CNBC. He pointed to the "human-intensive" nature of manufacturing, and the time it can take to adapt production to a new design for a weapon or drone. "When a design changes, you can retrain a human in a day — but it takes three to six months in order to change the automation to reflect the new design," McGrew said. "We've built a software and AI product that basically allows manufacturing engineers to build assembly lines much faster." McGrew joined OpenAI in 2017 and worked on the reasoning capabilities of early models before the launch of ChatGPT. He left during a 2024 wave of other high-profile exits, including chief technology officer Mira Murati and co-founder and chief scientist Ilya Sutskever. "OpenAI is an amazing place," McGrew said. He said he remembers being in rooms with CEO Sam Altman , Dario Amodei, who left to start Anthropic , and Sutskever, "talking about what it would look like when a model could write your email for you." McGrew stayed through the famous weekend in November 2023 when Altman was abruptly fired and then rehired. McGrew said he wanted to stay to ship OpenAI's reasoning product, which he called the "last key breakthrough left before AGI," or artificial general intelligence. "I said, if I could just ship that, I'd be happy with my career at OpenAI, and I'd be ready to move on to something else," he said. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman delivers the keynote address during the OpenAI developers conference at Fort Mason on Sept. 29, 2026 in San Francisco, California. Heather Diehl | Getty Images McGrew, who hasn't spoken publicly about Arda until this week, said the company is using a combination of its own proprietary models, open-source models and some frontier models to run the software. Arda's other co-founders include Augustus Odena, who helped start Adept and previously worked at Google and Meta , and former Palantir engineers Alex Mark and Jakob Frick. Altimeter's Apoorv Agrawal led the recent funding round. He met McGrew when they both worked at Palantir. Manufacturing largely happens overseas, Agrawal said, but there's a market for bringing it back. "Manufacturing globally is a $16 trillion industry. In the U.S. alone, it's $3 trillion," Agrawal said. "We think that Arda, and the vision that they've outlined, will continue to capture a significant portion of that. Yes, the price is steep today, but the long-term opportunity is very high." McGrew said robotics is next on the product roadmap, and automating factories could help bring more manufacturing — and more jobs — to the U.S. "If your design changes very frequently, the only place you can really build your product is in East Asia, because you need an army of human workers who can be retrained quickly, and you can't wait for automation to catch up," he said. McGrew also highlighted the economic opportunity as the Trump administration looks to onshore manufacturing. "No one has ever successfully built a smartphone in the U.S.," he said. "Never successfully assembled one, and so if you can build a smartphone in the U.S. that is not taking away American jobs. That is bringing American jobs." texts.https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/20/spotif: Spotify on Tuesday launched paid memberships, a new way for podcasters to make money from their biggest fans beyond paywalled bonus episodes. Creators can decide which perks to offer listeners, which could be bonus audio or video, fewer ads, early access to shows, or some combination of these. The streaming service first previewed the idea at its Investor Day in May, where it also introduced AI capabilities that let listeners ask questions about what they’re listening to or watching and debuted new tools for managing creator sponsorships. Image Credits: Spotify As the company explained at the time, memberships would help to “create a natural path to go deeper, unlocking new and exclusive experiences for fans and new revenue opportunities for creators.” The feature is now rolling out to 34 markets globally , including the U.S. The launch is the latest example of Spotify’s effort to make its platform more attractive to podcast creators, particularly as it moves further into the video space to compete with YouTube. Though podcasters have long been able to monetize through ads, the new memberships could entice more fans to support creators by offering more than just an occasional bonus episode. Creators keep 90% of the membership revenue and can package their benefits across multiple tiers and pricing options to appeal to fans at different levels of commitment. To qualify, podcasters must host their shows on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and at least three published episodes. Image Credits: Spotify Fans will see memberships promoted on the show’s Spotify page, where they can subscribe, pay, and immediately access the exclusive content. (The company tells us that memberships will be purchased on the web, not through in-app purchases). A handful of shows will offer memberships at launch, including “The Adam Friedland Show,” “Making Sense with Sam Harris,” “Shawn Ryan Show,” “The Sculpt Society,” “Two Hot Takes,” as well as YMH Studios, which is bringing memberships to 12 shows across its network. Memberships join other Spotify monetization tools, including advertising and the Spotify Partner Program, as well as features that help creators grow their audience, like promotions, free trials, and analytics. Soon, Spotify says creators will be able to offer fans membership badges and welcome clips, too. texts.https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/20/apple-ad: Apple adds U.S. titanium supplier for iPhone Duo Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Apple is adding a U.S. titanium supplier for its new iPhone Duo and expanding domestic production of camera components for the iPhone 18 Pro. It's part of the company's push to manufacture more critical components in the U.S. Apple said it's committing up to $100 million over three years to Pennsylvania-based Perryman Company, which will produce titanium used in Apple products including the $1,999 iPhone Duo. In this article AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The new foldable iPhone Duo is displayed during an Apple event at the Steve Jobs Theater in Apple Park in Cupertino, California, on September 9, 2026. Apple unveiled its long-awaited first foldable smartphone, the iPhone Duo, on Wednesday, at the company's first launch event since CEO John Ternus took the reins on September 1. Apple's first foldable comes seven years after Samsung pioneered the category, but the American tech giant is expected to take a sizable chunk of the market. (Photo by Karl Mondon / AFP via Getty Images) Karl Mondon | Afp | Getty Images Apple is adding a U.S. titanium supplier for its new iPhone Duo and expanding domestic production of camera components for the iPhone 18 Pro as part of a push to expand manufacturing in its home country. The company said Tuesday it will commit up to $100 million over the next three years to Perryman Company, based in Houston, Pennsylvania, for the production of titanium used in Apple products, including the $1,999 foldable Duo. watch now VIDEO 2:28 02:28 Apple expands U.S. manufacturing footprint with new iPhone suppliers Squawk Box Since the start of President Donald Trump's second term, Apple has been vocal about its efforts to invest more in the U.S., even as the final assembly of most iPhones remains overseas. In August of last year, Apple launched the American Manufacturing Program (AMP), increasing its plan for domestic spending by $100 billion to a total of $600 billion. Tim Cook , Apple's CEO until last month, appeared at the White House for that announcement, as Trump was pushing the iPhone maker and other tech giants to bolster production in the U.S. The latest announcement comes as Apple faces severe supply constraints for its first foldable phone, which goes on sale in stores Friday. Apple said Friday that preorder demand had been "nothing short of extraordinary," but hasn't said whether it plans to increase production. JPMorgan analysts estimate Apple will ship roughly 8 million to 9 million Duo devices this year, below earlier expectations of about 10 million, because of supply constraints. Apple didn't say whether the agreement with Perryman would increase near-term capacity. Perryman will melt, forge, and roll grade 5 titanium, which Apple said will contain at least 80% recycled material. Titanium is used for the Duo's enclosure, providing durability, according to Apple. Perryman Company employees handle spools of titanium used in iPhones as part of the American Manufacturing Program. Apple In addition to the Perryman announcement, Apple said Tuesday that it's expanding its partnership with Delaware-based Qnity Electronics , which will manufacture advanced films used in the variable-aperture camera system on the iPhone 18 Pro. The feature allows the phone's main camera to adjust how much light enters the lens depending on conditions, giving users greater control over light and depth. Apple said nearly 100 components used in the iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro are produced by American companies across more than a dozen states. "We're thrilled to expand our work with companies producing advanced materials and components for our newest iPhone lineup right here in America," Sabih Khan, Apple's operating chief, said in a statement. Apple also highlighted investments with other AMP partners, including Broadcom for U.S.-made chips, Corning for specialty glass used in iPhones and Apple Watches, and Amkor , which is constructing a semiconductor packaging and testing facility in Peoria, Arizona. America is its sleeping twin AI Venture Capital Exclusive: Daytona, a startup building the ‘agentic cloud,’ valued at $1 billion in latest funding round By Jeremy Kahn Jeremy Kahn Editor, AI By Jeremy Kahn Jeremy Kahn Editor, AI October 20, 2026, 8:00 AM ET Daytona cofounder and CEO Ivan Burazin. Photo courtesy of Daytona Add Fortune on Google for similar content. Add us on Google Add us on Google AI agents need somewhere to work—and Ivan Burazin thinks the existing cloud providers aren’t the right answer. Now Burazin, the cofounder and CEO of Daytona, a San Francisco-based startup, has turned the idea of a new kind of cloud just for AI agents into a unicorn business. Recommended Video Daytona said Tuesday it has raised a $60 million Series B venture capital round at a $1 billion valuation. FirstMark led the round. It was joined by an A-list roster of Silicon Valley founders, including Stripe’s Patrick Collison, Shopify’s Tobi Lütke, Perplexity’s Aravind Srinivas, Quora’s Adam D’Angelo and Zoom’s Eric Yuan, plus strategic investors Qualcomm Ventures, Samsung Next and Okta Ventures. Burazin told Fortune that about $50 million of the round came from existing investors. The new funding brings the amount Daytona has raised to date to about $91 million. Why agents need their own computers An AI agent that writes and runs code, browses the web or operates business software needs to use a computer—either an actual machine, or a virtual one, running in the cloud. For many use cases, having a virtual machine is preferable—it allows the AI agent to operate even if the person running the agent shuts down their laptop, and because virtual machines can be configured with only the software and network access the agent needs to do a particular task and nothing more, it is generally a safer way to run AI agents. A virtual machine, or “sandbox” as they are sometimes called, minimizes the chance that the agent will run amok and take damaging unauthorized actions, or that an outside party could hijack the agent and get it to divulge sensitive data. Daytona was founded in 2023 by Burazin, Goran Draganić and Vedran Jukić to automate software development environments for large enterprises. When the founders saw that agents would need computers too, Burazin said, they “basically gave our competitors all our customers, rebuilt everything, had like three months left of revenue in the bank, and then relaunched this thing.” Daytona currently provides these sandboxes to many of the leading AI companies, which use the virtual machines to allow their models to practice tasks over and over inside sandboxes during training and testing. Daytona says AI data company Snorkel, which also helps customers test and benchmark AI models, has provisioned more than one million sandboxes on its platform. It also counts Anthropic, OpenAI, Nvidia , Cursor, Cognition, Meta and Cohere among its customers. Burazin said that Daytona’s revenue run rate grew 25-fold between January and September. “We’ve been growing on average every single month 50.9%,” Burazin said. Existing cloud providers, such as Amazon’s AWS, Microsoft’s Azure, or Google’s Google Cloud Platform, allow customers to spin up virtual machines. But doing so takes between 30 seconds and many minutes, depending on the complexity of the configuration. This, Burazin said, is far too long for the future of agentic work, when companies may be deploying thousands or even tens of thousands of AI agents, each of which may need access to different software tools depending on the task they are being asked to complete. Daytona can configure a new sandbox for an AI agent in 60 milliseconds, according to Burazin. That is roughly half the time it takes to blink. The trick, he said, is to pre-distribute snapshots of configured machines onto the physical drives of servers. When an agent needs a machine, Daytona attaches processing power and memory and resumes the snapshot. Agents can also clone a running computer to try different approaches in parallel. “You can literally replicate the computer into two and try both outcomes, and then replicate again and again and again until it gets the desired outcome,” Burazin said. When he pitched investors, Burazin said, many asked “why the hell do we need this? You know, AWS can do this thing.” His answer is that hyperscalers built nearly everything on a few core services optimized for maximum utilization. To match Daytona’s performance, he argued, they would need to create a whole new company inside their existing cloud services. He conceded the hyperscalers could do this, but said it would not be easy for them to rebuild their infrastructure to serve AI agents instead of human users. The scale involved is easy to underestimate. Burazin pointed to Muse, the personal agent Meta launched in September. He said it has “a computer underneath for every single chat.” By his back-of-the-envelope math, Muse would need $2.8 billion worth of sandboxes to serve 100 million users. “We believe the next infrastructure shift is from human-centric cloud primitives to agent-native ones,” Matt Turck, a partner at FirstMark, said in a statement. AI models run on GPUs. But to do work, they need CPUs. Burazin also distinguishes what Daytona is building from the “neocloud” providers such as CoreWeave and Nebius. Those neoclouds are designed to train and run AI models. The data centers they are standing up are stuff full of graphics processing units, or GPUs, the computer chips optimized to run AI models. But to run virtual machines, a data center needs lots of traditional central processing units, or CPUs, that can run all kinds of different software. “The inference clouds is where the agent thinks, and our cloud is where the agent works,” Burazin said. “We internally sort of believe that the number of dollars spent on CPUs will probably be higher than the dollars spent on GPUs in the foreseeable future,” he said, “which seems sort of counterintuitive today.” The demand is so great that he forecasts a coming CPU shortage. “I strongly believe that there will be a CPU crunch,” he said. “The amount of CPU machines that we will need if we want to keep growing at this trajectory actually doesn’t exist right now.” Chipmakers are seeing the same trend. On AMD’s first-quarter earnings call in May, CEO Lisa Su said agentic AI was increasing the need for server CPUs. AMD raised its forecast for server CPU market growth from about 18% a year to more than 35%, reaching over $120 billion by 2030. Chip designer Arm has estimated that agentic AI data centers could need 120 million CPU cores per gigawatt, four times what traditional data centers require. Intel told some Chinese customers earlier this year that lead times for certain server CPUs had stretched to six months, Quartz reported. Burazin said Daytona plans to spend most of the new funds it has raised on hiring go-to-market sales staff, plus some engineers.
